# Persistence

<!-- Generated by `npm run train` from the sources each rule cites. To change a rule for good, change its source or say so in training/feedback.md; the next training run regenerates this file. -->

- **Make related writes that must succeed or fail together, such as a multi-part provisioning operation or creating an account with its principal and identity, in one unit of work with a single save. Don't call save between creating related entities, and don't keep earlier saves after a later step fails validation.** If a later step fails after an earlier save, the data is left half-written, for example an administrator saved without the client registration that was refused. *Check:* Look for several SaveChanges calls or separate transactions in one operation that creates or changes dependent entities, and for related entities created lazily on a later read or login. *Note:* Exceptions: an operation whose decision record accepts per-step saves and a rerun that finishes the work (see the related do-not-report rule), and swapping an active row under a filtered unique index (see that rule). <sub>NCodeGroup maintainer: principal-engineer-review; Identity ADR-1512; Identity ADR-1057; Identity ADR-1192</sub>
- **A store method, or a helper called inside an existing unit of work, stages its changes on the caller's store manager or unit of work and never calls SaveChanges itself, not even to back-fill a token. It never opens a second store manager or DbContext of its own. Committing belongs to the unit of work's owner, and a seed coordinator commits a seed once.** Several operations must be able to commit together. A second store manager commits outside the caller's transaction, leaves its precondition read out of that transaction and costs an extra connection. *Check:* Look for SaveChanges/SaveChangesAsync calls inside individual store methods, seed contributors or helpers, and for helpers that create a new store manager or DbContext while their caller already holds one. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity ADR-1166; Identity outcomes of #827</sub>
- **Never change rows that carry an interceptor-managed concurrency token with set-based ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete (sync or async) or raw bulk SQL. Load the matching rows, a bounded batch at a time, change or remove them through the change tracker, and save each batch as one unit of work. Leave rows already in the target state, such as already-revoked rows, unchanged.** Set-based statements bypass the change tracker and the concurrency-token interceptor, so the token isn't bumped and concurrent writers and other replicas miss the change. The EF Core InMemory provider doesn't support them either. *Check:* Look for ExecuteUpdate, ExecuteUpdateAsync, ExecuteDelete, ExecuteDeleteAsync or raw UPDATE/DELETE SQL in stores, including bulk revoke and prune paths, and for unbounded bulk removals. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity ADR-1020; Identity ADR-1199; Identity ADR-1217; Identity ADR-1218; Identity ADR-1222; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Update a shared stored record by compare-and-swap on the concurrency token read: pass a read-modify-write update function that the store applies to the record as stored and applies again after a lost race. Never write a value, payload or 'reconciled' marker computed from an earlier read outside that function.** Replacing a record with a value built from an earlier read overwrites a write that landed in between, for example a client added to a session or an approval that arrived during a poll. *Check:* Look for code that reads a record, rebuilds its payload and writes it back through a plain update or save, and for reconciliation writes that aren't conditioned on the token read at the start of the pass. <sub>Identity ADR-1222; Identity ADR-1412; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **When a save loses an optimistic-concurrency race, retry only by re-reading in a new unit of work, for a bounded number of attempts (three in total), and let the last concurrency exception propagate. Never resubmit the same entity without re-reading, retry in the same failed DbContext, loop without bound, or swallow the final failure.** Each attempt sees every write committed before it. Blind retries overwrite the other writer or fail again, unbounded loops can livelock, and swallowing hides the failure. *Check:* Look at catch blocks for concurrency exceptions: check for a fixed attempt limit, a fresh read and unit of work on each attempt, and a rethrow after the last attempt. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity ADR-1216; Identity ADR-1217; Identity ADR-1222; Identity ADR-1169</sub>
- **Make an operation whose outcome doesn't depend on what its caller read, such as a revocation, retry a lost concurrency race in production code instead of answering 412 Precondition Failed. Answer 412 only for a write conditioned on what the caller read, such as an If-Match update.** A revoke must always take effect, and a lost race doesn't mean the caller's request was wrong. *Check:* Look at single and bulk revoke paths and similar unconditional operations that save once and let a concurrency exception surface as 412 or as an error. <sub>Identity ADR-1020; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, a store reports a lost optimistic-concurrency race with its own store-neutral exception, named `StoreConcurrencyException`, never an Entity Framework type such as `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`. Handle it in one place: a management endpoint lets it propagate to a filter that answers 412.** Callers stay independent of the ORM, the same type has the same name in every NCodeGroup repository, and lost races are answered consistently. *Check:* Look for DbUpdateConcurrencyException caught or exposed outside the EF store, endpoints that catch the concurrency exception themselves, and store-neutral concurrency exceptions with another name such as `ConcurrencyConflictException`. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; project-template outcomes of #169</sub>
- **Regenerate row-level optimistic-concurrency tokens in one SaveChangesInterceptor, not by hand in each store's add and update methods. The interceptor overrides both SavingChanges and SavingChangesAsync through one shared implementation, always assigns a new token to Modified and Deleted entries, and assigns one to Added entries only when the token is empty.** Every save, sync or async, must change the row version. Hand-written token handling repeats in every store and new stores forget it. A new row can't conflict, and a caller may pre-seed its token. *Check:* Look for stores that generate token values for modified entities, and for SaveChangesInterceptor classes that override only one of the pair, skip Modified/Deleted entries, or overwrite a non-empty token on Added entries. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **When an update changes only an entity's child collection or a dependent record, mark the parent row changed (for example by assigning its concurrency token) so the interceptor regenerates its token. A change announced on a cache-invalidation channel must also change the row token first.** If the parent row isn't marked modified, its version doesn't change, so concurrent writers go undetected and token-based cache revalidation misses the change. *Check:* Look for store updates that only add, remove or change child items, such as an owner's secrets, without touching the parent's concurrency token, and for change announcements sent without bumping the row token first. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity ADR-1050; Identity ADR-1416</sub>
- **Don't mark a slice version column (a column that versions only one part of a row) with [ConcurrencyCheck] or IsConcurrencyToken, and don't let the row-token interceptor bump it. Set it only in the operation that changes that slice.** A slice column must change only when its slice changes, so consumers reload just that slice. Bumping it on every save, or putting it in every WHERE clause, is wrong. *Check:* Look for slice or section version properties that carry concurrency-token configuration, that an interceptor touches, or that an operation sets without changing the matching slice. <sub>Identity ADR-1012</sub>
- **After a write whose concurrency tokens the save pipeline regenerates, return, cache or build ETags from the row read back after the commit, never from the pre-write copy. An update method doesn't return the new token on its DTO; a create assigns its token up front and may return it, and a caller that updates re-reads the entity or answers 204.** The interceptor regenerates an update's token during save, after the store method returns, so a pre-write copy carries a stale token that breaks ETags, revalidation and polls. *Check:* Look for code that builds an ETag from the DTO an update returned, caches an entity read before its update or seed committed, or create methods that don't assign a token. <sub>Identity ADR-1012; Identity ADR-1166</sub>
- **Make a single-use operation, such as first-run setup or redeeming a one-time record, mark itself used in the same save as its effect, guarded by an optimistic concurrency token, and check that the stored payload is readable before marking it consumed.** A separate 'used' save lets a crash or race run the operation twice. An unreadable record must count as absent and must not change state. *Check:* Look for completion flags written in a separate SaveChanges or transaction, rows updated without a checked concurrency token, and consume paths that set a consumed flag or delete the row before decrypting or validating the payload. <sub>Identity ADR-1512; Identity ADR-1235</sub>
- **When rotating a refresh token, revoke the presented grant only if it is still active and store its successor in the same unit of work. Never use separate saves, and never use a revoke that succeeds silently when the grant was already revoked.** Otherwise two concurrent refreshes can both get tokens, so reuse goes undetected, and a lineage revocation can run before the successor exists and leave it active. *Check:* Look at refresh-token rotation code for revocation and insertion in separate SaveChanges calls or transactions, and for a revoke whose result doesn't show whether the grant was active. <sub>Identity ADR-1216</sub>
- **Make a best-effort update, such as sliding a grant's expiration or touching a session's last-activity time, tolerate a lost concurrency race: keep the other request's change or drop the touch after its retries instead of failing the request. Throttle such touches (for example at most once a minute) rather than writing on every request.** Concurrent requests that each slide an expiry shouldn't fail, because the other request's change is acceptable, and writing on every call wastes writes. *Check:* Look for expiry or activity updates whose concurrency exception reaches the caller, that write on every request, or that overwrite the record without a concurrency-checked read-modify-write. <sub>Identity ADR-1216; Identity ADR-1220</sub>
- **Publish audit or domain events, cache-invalidation announcements and other external effects of a persisted change only after its unit of work commits, through a run-after-commit hook. Send an effect that must survive a crash (message, webhook, notification) through an outbox written in the same transaction and delivered at least once by a background worker with back-off to an idempotent handler.** A lost race or rollback discards the change but not an event already sent, so the trail would record changes that never happened. A retried attempt's discarded post-commit steps must never run, and a direct send after commit can be lost. *Check:* Look for event, audit or message calls made before SaveChanges/commit or inside the transaction, and for must-happen effects sent directly after commit without an outbox. <sub>Identity ADR-1404; Identity ADR-1166; Identity docs/audit-records.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Announce a change to other replicas from a `finally` block that follows the local cache eviction or seed, so the announcement is sent even when the eviction, seed or token bump fails.** Other replicas that don't learn of the change keep serving stale state. *Check:* Look for change handlers where a throwing eviction, seed or token regeneration would skip the broadcast or invalidation message. <sub>Identity ADR-1351; Identity ADR-1416</sub>
- **Don't destroy external resources, such as KMS keys, inside the transaction that removes their stored references; report what was removed and destroy it after the commit. When the server creates an external resource and the store then fails to add or commit its record, including a lost race, destroy the created resource before the failure propagates.** Destroying before commit loses resources still referenced if the transaction rolls back, and a failed write after creation leaves an orphaned resource. *Check:* Look for remote deletes inside a store transaction, and for remote creation followed by a store add/commit with no compensating destroy on failure. <sub>Identity ADR-1471; Identity ADR-1476</sub>
- **An orphaned-resource sweep lists the external provider's resources before it reads the stored references, and destroys only resources created at or before now minus a grace period.** Listing first means a resource recorded during the pass is never swept, and the grace period protects a creation still in flight before its record commits. *Check:* In sweep or garbage-collection code, check the order of the remote listing and the stored-reference read, and that a creation-time cutoff with a grace period is applied. <sub>Identity ADR-1478</sub>
- **Do expensive or external calls, such as a KMS wrap, before the window between two dependent database writes, not inside it.** An external call inside the window lengthens the time the data is between states and adds a failure point there. *Check:* Look for external crypto or network calls placed between two writes that must happen close together. <sub>Identity ADR-1407</sub>
- **When swapping an active row under a filtered unique index, retire the old row in one unit of work and insert the successor in another, both with concurrency tokens checked, and re-activate the old row if the insert fails. Don't rely on EF Core ordering the update before the insert in one SaveChanges.** EF Core doesn't guarantee statement order, so a single unit of work can violate the unique index. *Check:* Look for code that deactivates and inserts rows under a unique 'active' filter in one SaveChanges call, or that has no compensation when the insert fails. <sub>Identity ADR-1407</sub>
- **When a plan applies several changes to the same stored record, build each change from the record as the earlier changes left it, not from the copy the plan originally read.** A later change built from the original record writes the earlier change's fields back and silently undoes it, for example an extension that reverts an activation. *Check:* Look for apply loops that construct updates from the plan's captured record rather than from a working copy updated after each change, and for a missing test that combines two changes to one record. <sub>Identity ADR-1404; Identity outcomes of #551</sub>
- **A multi-step write that offers a preview runs every validation and authorization check in a planning phase before its first write, and the preview path writes nothing.** Then an apply fails only on a concurrent write or a fault, and running it again finishes an operation that stopped part way. *Check:* Look for validation, authorization or 403/409 decisions made after some writes in the apply step, and for any persistence call reached from the preview path. <sub>Identity ADR-1425</sub>
- **When a store deletes an owning entity, remove every dependent row it owns, including secrets, grants and tokens, consents and the role assignments its principal holds in any tenant, through the change tracker in the same unit of work. Answer 409 while the owner still holds records that belong to another party, and never let a foreign-key violation surface as 500.** With Restrict foreign keys a store that removes a row must also remove what references it, and one unit of work means a partial delete never leaves orphans or leftover grants that keep authorizing something that no longer exists. *Check:* Look for store delete methods that remove the parent but not its dependents, remove them in separate saves, filter dependents by the current tenant only, or let foreign-key exceptions bubble. <sub>Identity ADR-1212; Identity ADR-1192; Identity ADR-1466; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **An endpoint or handler that deletes an entity calls the store's remove method and relies on it to remove the dependents; it doesn't delete secrets, tokens or other dependents itself.** Removing dependents is the store's job in its own unit of work, and doing it in the endpoint splits that unit of work. *Check:* Look for endpoint or handler code that deletes dependent records before or after calling the store's remove method. <sub>Identity ADR-1212</sub>
- **Keep foreign keys `DeleteBehavior.Restrict` and remove dependents explicitly in the store; don't configure database cascade deletes.** SQL Server refuses multiple cascade paths, the InMemory provider cascades only tracked rows, some dependents reference their owner by identifier with no foreign key, and explicit deletion makes ownership visible. *Check:* Look for `OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Cascade)` or `ClientCascade` in model configuration, or migrations that add ON DELETE CASCADE. <sub>Identity ADR-1212; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **When an account or principal is deleted, end its sessions and send any notifications that need its data before removing that data, and pass the request's cancellation token to that step.** Once grants and consents are erased, the sessions can no longer be listed to notify their relying parties. *Check:* In delete paths, check that session termination comes before any store removal and isn't deferred to post-commit work. <sub>Identity ADR-1229</sub>
- **Apply tenant isolation once, as a global query filter targeting a tenant marker interface, on every tenant-bound entity, and give each such entity a denormalized, indexed tenant-ID column. Don't rely on each query passing the current tenant. When erasing a tenant, find its entity types from the EF model the same way, not from a hardcoded list.** Per-call-site scoping is correct only while every call site remembers it. A filter by interface scopes new entities, including those other packages contribute, automatically. *Check:* Look for tenant-bound entities that don't implement the marker interface or lack an indexed tenant column, queries that add their own tenant predicate instead of relying on the filter, filters that reach the tenant through a join, and tenant deletion that lists specific DbSets. <sub>Identity ADR-1018; Identity ADR-1212; Identity ADR-1411</sub>
- **Open the persistence tenant scope for a tenant-bound management route from the route's tenant identifier, not from the tenant resolved for the request, and return not-found when the route has none.** The scope is then the same under every hosting strategy, and the query filter fails closed if a handler forgets to filter. *Check:* Look for tenant-bound management routes outside a group that opens the tenant scope from the route value, or that proceed without a scope when the tenant identifier is missing. <sub>Identity ADR-1191</sub>
- **A lookup that bypasses the tenant query filter (`IgnoreQueryFilters()`) and returns a single row must match a value that a unique index guarantees across tenants, or fetch two rows and fail closed when more than one matches. Give such a query an index that leads with its filtered column, or pass the tenant so a composite index leading with the tenant column applies.** A first match on a per-tenant-unique value reads an arbitrary tenant's row and can wrongly allow or refuse an authorization decision, and a cross-tenant query without a usable index scans the whole table. *Check:* For each new `IgnoreQueryFilters()` query, check FirstOrDefault/SingleOrDefault against the unique indexes, and compare its predicate columns with the entity's indexes. <sub>Identity outcomes of #629</sub>
- **Don't ask for an index to lead with the tenant column when the same index also serves a query that runs across tenants with `IgnoreQueryFilters()`.** An index that leads with the tenant column can't serve the cross-tenant query, while one without it serves both. *Check:* Before reporting a missing leading tenant column, search for other queries on the same columns that use `IgnoreQueryFilters()`. <sub>Identity outcomes of #629</sub>
- **Never lowercase or otherwise case-normalize an opaque, case-significant key such as a Base64Url hash or session id; store, index and match it verbatim. Add a normalized companion column with its own index only for a value whose match should be case-insensitive.** Base64Url is case-significant, so case folding lets distinct values collide and lowercased lookups miss the stored key. A companion column only exists to make a case-insensitive lookup use an index. *Check:* Look for ToLowerInvariant/ToUpperInvariant, case-insensitive comparisons or Normalized* columns on hashed keys or session ids, and for case-insensitive lookups on raw columns with no normalized, indexed companion. <sub>Identity ADR-1052; Identity ADR-1112</sub>
- **When a case-sensitive value is filtered through a case-folded normalized column, treat the database filter as a widening pre-filter and re-apply the exact ordinal match in memory; keep exact predicates such as booleans and id-set membership in the database.** The normalized column never drops a true match, but values such as OAuth scopes (RFC 6749) and resource indicators (RFC 8707) compare case-sensitively. *Check:* Look for queries on Normalized* columns whose results are used without an exact ordinal comparison, and for exact predicates evaluated in memory. <sub>Identity ADR-1080</sub>
- **Implement a filtered read as an intent-named store method that filters in the database query and projects only the columns the caller needs. Never page through or load a whole set and filter it in memory, and use generic paging such as GetPageAsync only for genuinely unfiltered lists.** Fetch-then-filter uses no index, transfers every row and child collection only to discard most, and the waste compounds when several readers re-scan the same set. *Check:* Look for callers that page or list a store and then apply Where or loops to find a subset, and for reads that return full entities with included child collections when the caller uses a few fields. <sub>Identity ADR-1080; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't expose IQueryable or Expression parameters on a store interface.** They tie the contract to an ORM, let callers shape the SQL, and force a non-EF backend to interpret expression trees. *Check:* Look for store interface methods that take or return IQueryable<T> or Expression<Func<...>>. <sub>Identity ADR-1080; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **A query that only needs owners, keys or identifiers projects just those columns instead of loading full rows, especially rows that carry wrapped key material or other secrets.** Loading whole rows moves secret material out of the database and wastes memory on every pass. *Check:* Look for store reads that return full entities with secret or large columns when the caller only uses identifier fields. <sub>Identity outcomes of #553; Identity ADR-1080</sub>
- **Don't query per item inside a loop (N+1) or append one Where clause per item of a pre-loaded list. Load related data in one query or bounded batches, and express exclusion of related rows as one server-side subquery such as `!db.Set<T>().Any(...)`.** Per-item queries multiply round trips, and per-item predicates grow the SQL and its parameter count with the data until they exceed provider limits. *Check:* Look for repository calls or lazy-loaded navigations inside loops over results, loops that add `.Where(...)` per element, lookup lists re-read on every page, and token reads done one identifier at a time or by loading the whole table. <sub>NCodeGroup maintainer: principal-engineer-review; Identity outcomes of #599; Identity ADR-1416</sub>
- **Within one request, resolve related data in the store manager or unit of work already open for the main read instead of opening a second one from a mapping or projection function.** A second store manager costs every request an extra context, connection and query, and the two reads don't share a unit of work. *Check:* Look for store-manager or DbContext factory calls such as `CreateAsync` inside mapping lambdas, or after another store manager was already used for the same request. <sub>Identity outcomes of #839</sub>
- **Don't report an entity as loaded several times in one operation when the callers share one DbContext and the store's lookup checks `DbSet.Local` before querying, and don't ask to remove an `Include` that the entity mapping function reads or that sibling lookups returning the same model also load.** Later lookups come from the change tracker, and the mapper needs those navigations to build the returned model. *Check:* Before reporting, check whether the callers share a store manager and the lookup consults `DbSet.Local`, and read the mapping function to see which navigations it accesses. <sub>Identity outcomes of #599; Identity outcomes of #839</sub>
- **Don't report a DbContext that defaults to QuerySplittingBehavior.SplitQuery as a round-trip regression when it keeps a host's explicit UseQuerySplittingBehavior choice and individual queries can call AsSingleQuery().** A single query joining several collections multiplies their rows as data grows, while a split query costs a bounded round trip per collection and can be opted out of. *Check:* Before reporting, confirm the context respects a host-chosen splitting behavior and that the AsSingleQuery() opt-out is documented. <sub>Identity outcomes of #832</sub>
- **Implement keyset paging over an index whose leading columns match the filter and sort: order by the surrogate key, or by a timestamp with a unique surrogate identifier as tie-breaker, fetch `limit + 1` rows to detect a next page, and encode the last item's sort values as an opaque Base64Url cursor. Treat a malformed cursor as the start of the list instead of failing.** Page cost stays constant, rows with equal timestamps are neither skipped nor repeated, and a stale or tampered cursor restarts the list instead of causing an error. *Check:* Compare each paged query's OrderBy and cursor predicate with the entity's indexes; look for missing tie-breakers, offset paging, cursors that throw or return 400 when malformed, and stores that reimplement the shared paging mechanics. <sub>Identity ADR-1014; Identity ADR-1303; Identity review of #420; Identity ADR-1223</sub>
- **Don't keyset-paginate over a string column whose sort order depends on the database collation; page by a key whose ordering the database guarantees.** If comparison and ordering disagree under the collation, a page boundary skips or repeats rows. *Check:* Look for paged queries that order by and filter `> lastValue` on a text column such as a path or name. <sub>Identity ADR-1426</sub>
- **Read background batches and paged walks as bounded keyset pages until the next cursor is null, each page an untracked (`AsNoTracking`) query in its own short unit of work; don't hold one context or transaction open for the whole walk.** Memory and tracked-entity state stay bounded however large the data is, and each query stays cheap. *Check:* Look for background queries that load all matching rows at once, walks that reuse one tracked DbContext across all pages, or read-only page queries without AsNoTracking. <sub>Identity ADR-1223; Identity ADR-1426; Identity ADR-1407</sub>
- **Don't ask individual stores to clamp a page limit when they page exactly as the shared base store does and caller-supplied limits are already bounded at the API edge.** A clamp belongs to the paging contract of every store, not a few of them. *Check:* Before reporting, compare the store's paging with the base store's and check whether the API edge normalizes the limit. <sub>Identity outcomes of #553</sub>
- **Give a table that grows with use a configured retention, enforced by a periodic hosted service that runs on a PeriodicTimer created from the registered TimeProvider and removes rows in bounded batches, each its own unit of work, repeating while a batch comes back full. Log any failure other than host shutdown and retry at the next tick, so only the stopping token ends the loop.** One unbounded delete holds a transaction and change tracker over everything past retention, and a transient failure must not end retention enforcement for the rest of the process lifetime. *Check:* Look for new growing tables without retention, single queries removing all expired rows, Task.Delay or the system clock instead of TimeProvider, and catch blocks that let a non-cancellation exception end the loop. <sub>Identity ADR-1199; Identity ADR-1218; Identity ADR-1303; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **In a batched prune, treat a batch whose save lost a concurrency race to another replica's prune as a full batch and continue, rather than as an error that stops the prune.** Every replica prunes without leader election, so concurrent prunes are expected; the rows are already gone and more may be waiting. *Check:* Look at how a prune loop handles DbUpdateConcurrencyException or the store-neutral concurrency exception: it should continue the loop, not abort or log an error. <sub>Identity ADR-1218; Identity ADR-1303</sub>
- **Give a store method that stages a bounded batch for removal a limit parameter guarded with ArgumentOutOfRangeException when below one, order the batch by a stable key before Take(limit), and return how many rows it staged.** A stable order and a returned count let the caller tell a full batch from the last one. *Check:* In batch-removal store methods, check for the guard (for example `ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfLessThan(limit, 1)`), an OrderBy before Take, and a returned count. <sub>Identity ADR-1218</sub>
- **Don't let a retention prune remove a record whose required termination or cleanup step hasn't run; measure retention from the time of that step, not from the record's expiry.** Otherwise a session could disappear without being terminated, leaving its grants active and its relying parties unnotified. *Check:* Check that the prune's selection requires the record to be revoked or terminated and measures retention from that time. <sub>Identity ADR-1223</sub>
- **Index the columns that a prune, scheduled or polling query filters on, unless the table is documented as small by design.** Without the index each pass scans a table that grows with use. *Check:* For new background queries filtering on columns such as RevokedWhen or ExpiresWhen, check the entity configuration or migration for a matching index. <sub>Identity ADR-1218; Identity outcomes of #572; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't ask for a new index for an unbounded predicate on a rarely run operation, such as a delete, when sibling stores already use the same pattern under a recorded decision.** An index is warranted only when that operation at scale needs it. *Check:* Before reporting, check how often the operation runs and whether sibling stores use the same predicate. <sub>Identity outcomes of #585</sub>
- **In production code, make a write that a background loop retries idempotent: record an identity in the same unit of work and skip writes whose identity exists, for example a per-writer batch number checkpoint for counters, or a unique key on each inserted record. A batch writer keeps a failed batch and writes it first on the next flush.** A save can commit and still report failure, so a blind retry adds counts or records twice, and billing-like data must not overcount. *Check:* Look for retried flushes that increment counters or insert records without a checkpoint or unique key saved in the same transaction, and for failed batches that are discarded. <sub>Identity ADR-1199; Identity ADR-1303; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Make seed and provisioning handlers idempotent and reconciling: look up existing data before writing, replace and log a record that differs from the current configuration instead of returning early, guard a seed that can run on several replicas with a concurrency token, and retry it in a fresh unit of work. Seed from host handlers, not from migrations or the migration worker. A seed handler that changes shared working state updates the seed context's copy so later handlers see it.** Seeds rerun on every start or cache miss and can race across replicas; add-only seeding never applies changed configuration, and non-idempotent seeds duplicate or corrupt data. *Check:* Look for seed handlers that insert unconditionally, return as soon as a record with the same id exists, lack a concurrency check, retry in the same DbContext, or live in migrations. <sub>Identity ADR-1073; Identity ADR-1166; Identity ADR-1169; Identity outcomes of #606</sub>
- **Code that must see a write just committed, such as a seed, a preview or a validation, reads the committed record from the store, not a cached copy refreshed by polling. Don't put a cache or invalidation seam under store reads; layer any cache on top of the unchanged store contract.** On the replica that committed, the polled copy may not be refreshed yet, and correctness must never depend on cache freshness. *Check:* Look for post-write reads that go through a polled or cached provider, and store interfaces gaining cache or invalidation parameters. <sub>Identity ADR-1204; Identity ADR-1080</sub>
- **A cached object materialized from a store row carries that row's concurrency token, and records the tokens of other entities it was built over, so its staleness can be detected.** Revalidation needs the token each cached copy was built from, and a dependent object can outlive the parent's cache entry. *Check:* Flag new cached domain objects that drop the row token, or revision reports that omit parent entities the object depends on. <sub>Identity ADR-1416</sub>

- **Where the repository tracks changes and has deployed releases, write schema migrations expand-only so the previous release keeps working during the rollout and after a rollback: add tables, nullable or defaulted columns and indexes; never drop, rename, retype, narrow or make required anything the previous release uses, or add unique, primary-key, check or foreign-key constraints to an existing table, in the same release.** Migrations run before each rollout while the previous release still serves traffic, and EF writes explicit NULL for columns it maps as nullable. *Check:* In migration files, look for DropColumn, DropTable, RenameColumn, RenameTable, AlterColumn to non-nullable or narrower types, required columns without defaults, and new unique indexes or constraints on existing tables. *Note:* In a repository whose conventions say it is pre-release and tracks no changes, renames and format changes are allowed outright. <sub>Identity ADR-1134; Identity docs/hosting-analysis.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; NCodeGroup maintainer: principal-engineer-review</sub>
